property_summary: For any caller/address, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer after initialize), whereas the mutant returns address(0) breaking that invariant for inputs where the stored owner is non-zero.

For any caller, the reference contract's owner() always returns the internally stored _owner address (the actual owner), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns msg.sender, so there exists a caller for which owner() differs from the stored owner.

The correct contract's owner() getter always returns the stored owner address (the deployer after initialize), whereas the mutant incorrectly makes owner() return address(this), so for some initialized owner addresses the returned value will differ from the real stored owner.

For any nonzero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant that removes the nonzero check additionally allows setting owner to address(0) via transferOwnership, violating the rule that transferOwnership never sets owner to the zero address for nonzero inputs (and enabling owner==address(0) when newOwner==address(0)).

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never reverts and results in owner() equaling newOwner (including when newOwner equals the current owner, where the reference does a no-op), while the mutant rejects calls where newOwner == owner() by reverting.

For any caller that is the contract owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference never reverts and results in owner() equal to newOwner after the call (including when newOwner equals the current owner — it's a no-op), whereas the mutant reverts when newOwner == owner(), violating that owner() becomes equal to newOwner for that input.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract; the mutant reverts when newOwner == owner(), breaking this invariant for those inputs.

For any caller that is the owner and any non-zero newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference either succeeds and results in owner() == newOwner (including when newOwner equals current owner, treated as no-op), but the mutant additionally REVERTS when newOwner == owner() — so the general rule: if the caller is the owner and newOwner != address(0), transferOwnership never reverts; the mutant violates this for inputs where newOwner == owner().

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference either succeeds (and sets owner() to newOwner) or is a no-op when newOwner == owner() (i.e. it does not revert); the mutant additionally reverts when newOwner == owner(), so there exist inputs (caller == owner and newOwner == current owner) where the mutant reverts but the reference never reverts — we assert that calling transferOwnership from the owner never reverts (ok == true).

Rule: Only the EOA that is the contract owner (owner() == msg.sender) can successfully call transferOwnership; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a contract caller (forwarder) to invoke transferOwnership when forwarded from the owner EOA, violating that only direct-owner-calls succeed for some inputs.

For every caller address X, only direct calls where msg.sender == owner() succeed to transfer ownership; a malicious forwarding contract that calls transferOwnership on behalf of the owner must be rejected by the reference but (for some fuzzed owner/forwarder) accepted by the mutant that compares tx.origin instead of msg.sender.

Only calls whose msg.sender equals the stored owner can invoke transferOwnership (reference: require(owner()==msg.sender)); the mutant that uses tx.origin allows a forwarding contract to succeed when tx.origin==owner even though msg.sender (the forwarder) is not the owner.

For any address input, the reference contract rejects setting roundImplementation to the zero address (the call reverts) while the buggy mutant allows updating roundImplementation to address(0), so the reference never ends up with roundImplementation == address(0) but the mutant can for some input.

For all inputs, a call to updateRoundImplementation(newRoundImplementation) on the correct contract either reverts when newRoundImplementation == address(0) or results in roundImplementation != address(0); the mutant allows setting roundImplementation to address(0) for some input, violating that invariant.

For all addresses passed to updateRoundImplementation, the reference contract never sets roundImplementation to address(0) (the call either reverts or results in a non-zero roundImplementation); the mutant allows updating roundImplementation to address(0) for some input, violating that invariant.

After any call to updateRoundImplementation(x) by the owner, the reference contract either reverts if x==address(0) or else stores roundImplementation==x (i.e., roundImplementation is non-zero after a successful call); the mutant can return successfully while leaving roundImplementation equal to address(0) for some input, violating that guarantee.

For every non-owner caller, updateRoundImplementation must revert (onlyOwner); the mutant still enforces onlyOwner, but for the owner: after a successful call by the owner, the reference never allows roundImplementation to be address(this) (i.e. owner cannot set implementation to the factory contract address) whereas the mutant can — so the property: for any owner caller and any candidate address impl, either the call reverts or c.roundImplementation() != address(c); the bug allows a successful call that sets roundImplementation == address(c) (or any address) including address(0) — we target that owner call that would set it to address(c) (deployed contract) which the reference disallows only because it requires non-zero and our test distinguishes by trying to set to address(c) which is non-zero, so we actually target that owner calls always succeed to set to the provided non-zero address; the mutant allows zero too, but to distinguish we assert that after any owner call with impl == address(c) the stored value equals address(c) (reference holds and mutant also holds) — to trigger the mutant we instead assert that calling with impl == address(0) must revert for the reference but may succeed for mutant; therefore we use a combined check: when called by owner with impl == address(0) the reference reverts (ok==false) — this is the invariant we assert.

For any owner caller and any address value passed to updateRoundImplementation, the reference contract sets roundImplementation to exactly the provided address (roundImplementation == newRoundImplementation); the mutant inverts the require and therefore will reject non-zero addresses and only allow zero, causing roundImplementation to differ for many inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any proposed newRoundImplementation address, the reference contract will accept and set roundImplementation to that exact address; the mutant instead only accepts the zero address, so for some non-zero addresses the stored roundImplementation will differ between reference and mutant.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any address value newRoundImplementation, calling updateRoundImplementation(newRoundImplementation) results in c.roundImplementation() equaling the passed newRoundImplementation (the reference always stores the provided value; the mutant only allows zero and therefore will differ for non-zero inputs).

For any caller who is the owner, calling updateRoundImplementation(newImpl) sets c.roundImplementation() equal to the provided newImpl; the mutant that stores msg.sender instead will make roundImplementation != newImpl for some inputs (when owner != newImpl).
